source: Zhang et al. (2025) Scaf-GRPO: Scaffolded Group Relative Policy Optimization for Enhancing LLM Reasoning
finding: RL training stalls on problems the model always fails (zero reward, no gradient). Scaf-GRPO gives tiered in-prompt hints only when learning has plateaued, then the model must finish the solution itself. This is support-then-withdrawal inside training.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B, pass@1: AIME24 30.0 (vanilla GRPO) to 43.3 (relative +44.3%); 7-benchmark avg 45.2 to 50.9. Beats prefix-based LUFFY by 9.2% relative.
quote: strategically provides minimal guidance only when a model's independent learning has plateaued
limits: Training method (weights change), not inference-time scaffolding. Hints made by DeepSeek-R1 from ground-truth solutions. AIME24 has 30 items, so one item is 3.3 points.
agent_relevance: Hints are kept for true-hard items only; an agent could gate help on a failed check, which fits G1 (act on a signal) and G12 (spend by difficulty).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Scaf-GRPO: Scaffolded Group Relative Policy Optimization for Enhancing LLM Reasoning (hint-hierarchy ablation)
finding: Three hint tiers, abstract to concrete: knowledge, planning, solution. Hints come one increment at a time, stopping at the first success. Removing parts of the ladder hurts.
numbers: Avg over 7 benchmarks (Qwen2.5-Math-7B): full 50.9; solution-hint only 48.4; no knowledge hint 49.2; no planning hint 48.6; no solution hint 48.0; no incremental chunking 47.7; no guidance 45.2.
limits: Gaps of 1-3 points on small benchmarks; no seeds or intervals in the table. One model family for the ablation.
agent_relevance: Supports a graded help ladder (concept, then plan, then step) over giving the answer. Echoes the least-support-that-works idea of contingent shifting in Wood, Bruner, Ross.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Scaf-GRPO: Scaffolded Group Relative Policy Optimization for Enhancing LLM Reasoning (guidance exemption period)
finding: Hints are held back for the first part of training so the model tries alone first. Starting scaffolds from step 0 hurts (hint dependency). Result is stable for exemption of 10% to 40% of training.
numbers: Scaffolding from the very start: 9.2% relative drop vs full method. Exemption 10-40% gives 49.5%-50.9% avg; 15% chosen. Also +10.3% relative over GRPO on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and +5.9% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B.
quote: applying scaffolding from the very beginning leads to a 9.2% relative performance drop
limits: Gain shrinks for the stronger long-CoT model (5.9% vs 44.3% on AIME24 for the math base model), a mild expertise-reversal pattern; not tested directly.
agent_relevance: Try alone first, then help: a machine echo of the guided-discovery debate. Suggests S3 first attempts stay unscaffolded, with S5/S6 adding help.

source: Li et al. (2026) QuestA: Expanding Reasoning Capacity in LLMs via Question Augmentation
finding: Adds a fraction of the reference solution to hard training prompts so RL gets non-zero reward. Then reduces the fraction: 50% hint, then 25% hint. Improves pass@1 and pass@k.
numbers: Nemotron-1.5B: AIME24 61.77 to 72.50, AIME25 49.50 to 62.29, HMMT25 31.56 to 41.67, avg 53.14 to 63.26. Partial-50 stage only: avg 60.26. 26K augmented prompts.
quote: the model transitions from scaffolded reasoning to autonomous reasoning
limits: Fade has two steps, not a smooth curve. Extending to 0% hint gave no gain. Partial-25 was about as hard as no hint, so it may add little itself. Reference solutions come from the training set.
agent_relevance: Support-then-withdrawal with a stated rationale: train toward the no-hint test distribution. Hint size works as a difficulty knob usable for S6 subgoal help.

source: Li et al. (2026) QuestA (easy prompts and pass@k)
finding: RL on easy prompts lowers pass@k at large k; RL on hard prompts raises it but learns slowly. Hints make hard prompts learnable.
numbers: After QuestA the number of AIME24 problems unsolved at pass@32 fell from 5 to 2 (newly solved indices 2, 13, 29).
limits: Tiny item counts; one model.
agent_relevance: Matches G12: effort helps only where there is a foothold; a scaffold lifts a problem into reach (ZPD-like idea).

source: SEELE authors (2025) Staying in the Sweet Spot: Responsive Reasoning Evolution via Capability-Adaptive Hint Scaffolding
finding: Hint length is set per problem by fitting an item-response-theory model on earlier rollouts, aiming at about 50% rollout accuracy. This keeps each problem in the learner's sweet spot (ZPD-like).
numbers: Six math benchmarks avg: Qwen2.5-3B SEELE 42.2 vs GRPO 30.4 vs best baseline UFT 40.5; Qwen2.5-1.5B 34.2 vs 24.2 vs 30.4. General reasoning (3B): 53.2 vs 51.0. Target accuracy 0.5 best, falling off symmetrically.
quote: SEELE augments each training sample by appending a hint (part of a full solution) after the original problem.
limits: No fixed-hint-length baseline, so the gain from adapting (vs fading on a schedule) is not isolated. Small models, 400 steps, one dataset (DeepMath-103K hard subset). Page read via WebFetch summary.
agent_relevance: Adaptive per-item help sized to measured success; code, not the model, sets the help level.

source: Macina, Daheim, Hakimi, Kapur, Gurevych, Sachan (2025) MathTutorBench
finding: Benchmark for LLM tutors: problem solving, mistake detection, scaffolding generation, pedagogical instruction following. Solving ability does not make a good tutor; pedagogy and expertise trade off by how specialised the model is.
numbers: Scaffolding score by a trained reward model, reported as win rate against human teacher replies; each task has a base and a hard split with longer dialogs (avg 5.78 turns). Human-rated pedagogical preference pairs lifted the reward model to about 0.8; synthetic GSM8K step data did not help.
quote: subject expertise, indicated by solving ability, does not immediately translate to good teaching
limits: Reward-model judge, not learning outcomes; math only; dialogs under 10 turns. Authors say it does not replace human learning studies.
agent_relevance: A scaffold-quality benchmark exists and could score S5 hint text. Strong solvers over-help; a tutor role needs its own instruction.

source: Macina et al. (2025) MathTutorBench (long dialogs, instruction following)
finding: Scaffolding quality drops on longer dialogs for most models; only LearnLM held steady. Most models gain little when told to follow a pedagogical instruction; GPT-4o gained, SocraticLM, LearnLM and Llama did not.
numbers: Win rate on the hard (longer) split is lower than on the base split for most tested models. Per-model values not recorded.
limits: Per-model table values not extracted; judged by an automatic reward model.
agent_relevance: Fading over a long loop is hard for models: track the support level in code across turns instead of asking the model to remember it.

source: Dinucu-Jianu, Macina, Daheim, Hakimi, Gurevych, Sachan (2025) From Problem-Solving to Teaching Problem-Solving: Aligning LLMs with Pedagogy using RL
finding: Online RL trains a 7B tutor against a simulated student. Reward: student solves the problem, with a lambda-weighted penalty for leaking the solution and low pedagogy score. Plain LLMs prioritise answering over teaching. Raising lambda trades student success for less leakage.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B tutor, student Llama-3.1-8B; student solve-rate gain: lambda=0.0 36.2%, 0.5 30.9%, 0.75 25.3%, 1.0 24.7%, 1.5 21.2%. At lambda=0 the tutor leaks answers. Reaches LearnLM-class pedagogy without human labels; MMLU, GSM8K, MATH500 preserved, unlike SocraticLM.
quote: even with engineered prompts, standard LLMs are inherently optimized for answering rather than teaching
limits: Simulated student and LLM judges for leakage and pedagogy (Gemma3-27B at test); no human learners. Solve-rate gain is on the simulated student only.
agent_relevance: Withholding the answer must be rewarded and checked by a leak detector. Our scaffold can test candidate hints for leaks before showing them.

source: LearnLM Team (2024) LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
finding: Pedagogy is cast as instruction following: system prompts state wanted teaching behaviour (for example offer scaffolds and hints as needed, do not solve for the student). Training on such data gives a tutor that experts prefer.
numbers: Expert preference strength +31% over GPT-4o, +11% over Claude 3.5 Sonnet, +13% over base Gemini 1.5 Pro. Role-playing learners favoured LearnLM when it stayed on topic and challenged them.
quote: you don't solve problems for your students, but you offer scaffolds and hints as needed
limits: Preferences of pedagogy experts and role-played learners, not real learning outcomes in this report; compared with 2024 models.
agent_relevance: A scaffold spec can be written as instructions (hint ladder, no answer) and graded by rubric.

source: Eedi and LearnLM study authors (2025) Exploratory RCT of tutor-supervised LearnLM vs human tutors and static hints
finding: 165 UK students (Years 9-10, 5 schools). LearnLM, prompted for short Socratic replies that do not reveal the answer, drafted tutor messages that a human approved or edited. Outcomes matched human tutors and beat static hints.
numbers: Mistake remediation: static hints 65.4%, human tutor 91.2%, LearnLM 93.0%. Misconception resolution: 86.8, 94.9, 95.4%. Transfer to next unit's first question: 56.2, 60.7, 66.2% (LearnLM vs human +5.5 pp, interval -1.4 to +12.4). Tutors accepted 74.4% of 3,617 drafts unedited; 5 factual errors (0.1%).
limits: Exploratory; human in the loop, so not autonomous; immediate effects only; maths only; transfer gap not conclusive. Tutors sometimes overrode the model when Socratic questions frustrated students. First 100,000 characters of the page read.
agent_relevance: Model hints work when a human or check gates them. Edits were mostly pacing (44.3%): how much support and when was the model's hardest part.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (PNAS 122(26) e2422633122)
finding: Field experiment in Turkish high school maths, nearly 1,000 students: GPT Base (plain chat), GPT Tutor (teacher input, hints not answers), control. Plain chat helped practice but hurt the exam; the hint-based tutor removed the harm. Read through a Wharton summary and a search snippet, not the paper (PNAS blocked).
numbers: Practice with AI: GPT Base +48%, GPT Tutor +127%. Exam without AI: GPT Base -17% vs control; GPT Tutor about equal to control.
limits: Secondary source; one school and subject, four 90-minute sessions. The scaffold avoided harm; it did not lift exam scores above control.
agent_relevance: Strong field evidence that withdrawal matters: answers given by the helper become a prop that fails when removed. The agent should not copy a helper's answer.

source: Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne, Ponti (2025) AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT (Sci Rep 15:17458)
finding: Harvard physics (N=194, crossover): a GPT-4-based tutor that walks students through each problem part in order, with step-by-step solutions in the prompt, beat in-class active learning on the post-test.
numbers: AI group median post-score 4.5 (N=142) vs active learning 3.5 (N=174); effect size 0.63 by regression, 0.73 to 1.3 SD by quantile regression; p<1e-8. 70% of AI students spent under 60 minutes; median 49. Engagement rated 4.1 vs 3.6.
quote: a system prompt could not reliably provide enough structure to scaffold problems with multiple parts
limits: One topic pair, one university; ceiling effect; no delayed test. The system prompt alone could not keep multi-part problems in order, so the platform enforced the order.
agent_relevance: The prompt failed to hold scaffold order; code had to enforce the sequence. Supports program decides, model fills the slot.

source: Wang, Ribeiro, Robinson, Loeb, Demszky (2024) Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
finding: RCT with 700+ tutors and 1,000+ students: an LLM gives human tutors expert-style suggestions in real time. Students were more likely to master topics; low-rated tutors gained most.
numbers: +4 percentage points topic mastery (p<.01; exit-ticket pass 62% to 66%); +9 pp for lower-rated tutors; about $20 per tutor per year; 350,000 messages analysed: more probing questions, less generic praise.
limits: Human tutors in the loop; exit tickets are short checks, not long-term retention.
agent_relevance: Scaffold helps the weakest most, a sign of expertise reversal: give less help to those who need less. Gate help by measured weakness.

source: Cohn et al. (2026) Evidence-Decision-Feedback: Theory-Driven Adaptive Scaffolding for LLM Agents (Copa)
finding: An LLM peer agent in a high school science class picks dialogue moves from logged evidence of mastery. Moves shift from probing to suggesting and pushing as mastery rises, and student requests for help fall.
numbers: n=33 dyads, 6 weeks, C2STEM kinematics. Spearman rho with mastery: PROBE_UNDERSTANDING -0.34 (p=0.034), SUGGEST_ACTION +0.33 (p=0.039), PUSH_LIMIT +0.42 (p=0.007); success explaining code rises with mastery (rho=0.40); agent-help requests fall (rho=-0.26), 59% of support while mastery below 40%.
limits: Correlational, no control group, small n, no learning-gain test. Fading shown as less probing, not less help overall. Copa stops probing above mastery 0.7.
agent_relevance: A working LLM agent loop with an evidence model and named policies that fade. Close to S0 mode choice plus code-driven moves.

source: Amanlou et al. (2026) Beyond Access: Guided LLM Scaffolding for Independent Learning in Undergraduate Statistics (ICCE 2026)
finding: Four-week quasi-experiment, 17 students per arm (No-LLM, Unrestricted, Guided with rules on stepwise hints and verification). Guided use changed how students asked; outcomes were only directional.
numbers: Process over answers 22% (unrestricted) to 100% (guided); stepwise hints 7% to 41% (p=.009). Practice scores: no consistent gain. Quiz 4 no-help: Guided beat No-LLM by 23.17 points (Hedges g=0.95, p=.022) and Unrestricted by 16.42 (g=0.73, p=.079). Final exam g=0.61 and 0.71, intervals include zero.
limits: Quasi-experimental, small n, exploratory contrasts, behaviour-defined groups.
agent_relevance: Assisted practice scores did not show the benefit; unaided scores did. Test with help removed (links to G3).

source: Fischer, Rau, Rilke (2025) AI Tutoring Enhances Student Learning Without Crowding Out Reading Effort (IZA DP 18338)
finding: Pre-registered experiment, 334 university students. Tested restricted AI access (read alone first) vs unrestricted. The expected benefit of forced independent first study did not appear.
numbers: AI access overall +0.23 SD; unrestricted +0.34 SD vs control; restricted +3.4% relative (not significant); unrestricted 5.1% above restricted; gains concentrated in lower-baseline, better self-regulating students.
limits: 25-minute lab session; short-term exam; GPT-4 RAG tutor with no strong pedagogical scaffold described.
agent_relevance: Counter-example: forced try-alone-first did not help. Weighs against a fixed rule to withhold help early (cf. Scaf-GRPO exemption); timing may be better driven by a signal.

source: Pardos and Bhandari (2024) ChatGPT-generated help produces learning gains equivalent to human tutor-authored help on mathematics skills
finding: Crowd workers learned algebra and statistics with no hints, human tutor hints, or ChatGPT hints. ChatGPT hints gave gains similar to human ones, but 32% failed human quality checks.
numbers: N=274 analysed of 394: 90 control, 86 human, 98 ChatGPT. Gains: control 1.85% (ns), human 11.62% (p=.001), ChatGPT 17.00% (p<.001); ChatGPT vs control p=.011, vs human p=.416. Majority vote over 10 samples cut error to 0%, 2%, 2%, 13% by subject.
quote: ChatGPT-generated help failed quality checks on 32% of problems
limits: ChatGPT 3.5; MTurk adults, not students; 30% attrition; pre-test differences; equivalent means a non-significant difference, not an equivalence test.
agent_relevance: Hint correctness needs a check; majority vote over varied samples cut bad hints sharply. Only 100,000 characters of the page read.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Prompt in two stages: break the problem into easier subproblems, then solve them in order with earlier answers fed forward. A computational form of scaffolding by decomposition; it generalises to harder problems than the exemplars.
numbers: Last-letter concatenation, code-davinci-002, length 12: least-to-most 74.0% vs chain-of-thought 31.8%; standard prompting 0%. SCAN length split: at least 99% with 14 exemplars vs 16% chain-of-thought. GSM8K 62.39% vs 60.97%; problems needing 5+ steps 45.23% vs 39.07%.
quote: almost every problem in GSM8K that least-to-most prompting fails to solve can be eventually solved by using a manually crafted decomposition
limits: GSM8K gain small. Failures come from the decomposition; hand-made decompositions fix almost all. The scaffold is never faded.
agent_relevance: Shows a decomposition scaffold lifts length generalisation. In our schema it sits in S2/S6 subgoals; the weak spot is choosing the decomposition.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting (exemplar-matched control)
finding: Extra chain-of-thought exemplars barely close the gap: the decomposition, not the added words, adds the value on length generalisation.
numbers: Last-letter length 12: chain-of-thought 37.4% with 4 independent exemplars, 38.4% with 8, vs least-to-most 74.0%. DROP non-football 82.45 vs 74.77; football 73.42 vs 59.56.
limits: Main tables use code-davinci-002; newer models may need less scaffolding.
agent_relevance: A fair equal-effort control (G7): the effect remained after matching exemplar count.

source: Kim, Belland, Walker (2018) Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
finding: Older computational scaffolds (software prompts and hints in problem-based STEM) give a small to moderate gain. Fading is rarely used in the studies reviewed.
numbers: Overall g = 0.385 on cognitive outcomes (95% credible interval 0.022 to 0.802). Metacognitive g=0.384, strategic g=0.345, conceptual g=0.126. Earlier meta-analysis g=0.46. Fading used in 9.3% of 43 scaffolding articles in one review.
limits: Wide intervals; heterogeneous studies; Bayesian priors shape small subgroups. Pre-LLM software.
agent_relevance: A prior of g about 0.3-0.4 for software scaffolds; LLM-era effects (Kestin 0.63-1.3 SD; Tutor CoPilot +4 pp) are not directly comparable.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Scaf-GRPO (data filtering and hint quality)
finding: Authors scored hint quality (accuracy, minimality, clarity, coherence) and tie it to student performance; hints were written by an LLM from ground-truth solutions. Training on a harder filtered subset also helped.
numbers: Table 3 avg: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B Original GRPO 34.5 vs Scaf-GRPO 38.9; Filtered 35.6 vs 40.7. Qwen2.5-Math-7B Original 43.9 vs 48.4.
limits: Pass@1 on few benchmark items; filtered subsets chosen by authors.
agent_relevance: Hint text quality matters; the hint generator should see the reference or the check, as here, rather than guess.

source: Kirschner, Sweller, Clark (2006) Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work
finding: Human-side baseline claim that the LLM work now tests: novices learn more from full guidance than from discovery. Not read in depth by this agent; only the first page of a local copy was glanced at, so no figures are taken from it.
numbers: None taken.
limits: Review, not a meta-analysis. Machines are not novices in the same sense.
agent_relevance: Use as the baseline claim only; cite from the human-side evidence file.

source: Kalyuga and Renkl (2010) Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications
finding: Guidance that helps novices can hurt or waste effort for experts. Machine echo in this file: Scaf-GRPO gain was +44.3% (math base model) but +5.9% (long-CoT distilled model), and Tutor CoPilot helped low-rated tutors most. Only the first page was glanced at; the machine link is our reading.
numbers: None taken.
limits: Editorial of a special issue; machine links are not tested by the cited studies.
agent_relevance: S0 could choose less help for a model that already passes the check.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Scaf-GRPO (pseudo-hard filter and incremental delivery)
finding: Before giving any hint, Scaf-GRPO separates true-hard items from pseudo-hard ones that the model can solve alone with more training. Hints are then delivered in small increments, not whole levels at once.
numbers: Giving a whole hint level at once (Full Hint) cut performance by 6.3% relative to incremental delivery. Solution-only hints cut it by 4.9%. Hint-free exemption period chosen at 15% of training.
limits: Relative drops on a single 7B model; benchmark sets are small.
agent_relevance: Support should be the smallest step that works and should come after a solo try fails. In our loop: one extra check or hint chunk per round, never the full answer.
